To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
MET activation is not a suitable biomarker for resistance to EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitor (EGFR-TKIs), and that MET activation may enhance migratory and invasive ability of cancer cells.

MET activation may be an important factor that contributes to the acquisition of migratory and invasive properties by gefitinib-resistant lung cancer cells, although it does not seem to be a suitable marker of resistance to epithermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) tyrosine kinase (TK) inhibitors.

MET amplification was not found in gefitinib- or Erlotinib-resistant PC-9 cells; MET activation was found in gefitinb- or erlotini resistant PC-9 cells, but was not associated with sensitivity to these drugs; and MET activation may be a mechanism of resistance to EGFr inhibitors in lung cancer, but not the one investigated in this research.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of resistance to EGFP inhibitors.
the role of MET activation in determining the sensitivity of cancer cells to EGFR-TKI.
the mechanisms of resistance to EGFr-TKIs in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and the role of the MET receptor tyrosine in determining the sensitivity of NSCLC to EGFR-TKI therapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the MET gene amplification was a mechanism of escape to the anticancer effect by EGFR-TKI, but MET activation was not.

MET activation may be caused by various factors other than MET amplification and may enhance the migratory and invasive capabilities of cancer cells without affecting the sensitivity to EGFR inhibitors.
MET activation may be a mechanism for cancer cells to acquire migratory/invasive abilities, but is not a suitable marker for resistance to EGFR inhibitors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MET activation by factors other than gene amplification is a poor surrogate marker for resistance to EGFR TKIs, and MET activation by itself is not sufficient to confer resistance to EGFR inhibitors.
MET activation by itself is not a suitable marker for predicting resistance to EGFR TKIs, but MET may enhance migration and invasion ability in gefitinib- or Erlotinib-resistant cells.
MET activation by factors other than gene amplification is a poor predictor of sensitivity to EGFR TKIs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the activation of the MET receptor tyrosine kinases may be a mechanism of resistance to EGFG receptor tyrosine inhibitors in non-small cell lung cancer.
the MET pathway is activated in lung cancer patients who have acquired resistance to epidermoid growth factor receptor inhibitors (EGFR inhibitors).
MET activation may be an important mechanism in the development of resistance to EGGR-TKIs.
